youtube.aciklama:
In persistent tinnitus, the goal is not to erase the sound but to reduce its impact on daily life. In this lesson we cover education-based counseling, sound enrichment and sound generators, the role of hearing aids, the evidence for cognitive behavioral therapy, the stepped psychological approach of the NICE guideline and the treatments that guidelines do not recommend.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Tunkel et al., Clinical Practice Guideline: Tinnitus, Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (2014); NICE, Tinnitus: assessment and management (NG155, 2020); Fuller et al., Cognitive behavioural therapy for tinnitus, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (2020); Sereda et al., Sound therapy (using amplification devices and/or sound generators) for tinnitus, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (2018); Tyler, Tinnitus Handbook.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the management approaches used for bothersome tinnitus.
We will cover counseling, sound therapy, hearing aids and psychological treatments, each with its level of evidence.
Today there is no proven treatment that eliminates persistent subjective tinnitus.
So the goal of management is not to erase the sound but to reduce the impact of tinnitus on daily life.
The aim is for the person to live with tinnitus without distress, even when they notice it; this is called habituation.
Not everyone with tinnitus needs treatment; for tinnitus that is not bothersome, information is often enough.
For bothersome tinnitus, counseling, sound therapy, hearing aids and psychological treatments are considered together.
In this lesson we will look at what each approach does and where it stands in the guidelines.

maddeler.metin: What it is, why it happens
The sound is not a threat

cumleler: The foundation of all tinnitus management is education-based counseling.
American and British guidelines recommend giving information and support to people with tinnitus.
Counseling explains in plain language what tinnitus is, why it occurs and why it is not dangerous.
Explaining central gain and attention networks with simple analogies helps the person stop seeing the sound as a threat.
False beliefs, such as tinnitus being a sign of coming deafness or something that will never ease, are corrected.
The situations the person finds hardest, such as sleep or quiet rooms, are identified together and concrete goals are set.
Protection from noise matters, but wearing earplugs all the time, even in quiet places, can make tinnitus more noticeable.
Tinnitus is most noticeable in quiet surroundings and while falling asleep.
Instead of a completely silent bedroom, a soft background sound reduces the contrast between tinnitus and silence.
Sleep habits are also discussed, such as regular sleep hours and less screen use before bed.
Relaxation and breathing exercises can make tinnitus feel less bothersome when stress rises.
Continuing enjoyable activities helps move attention away from tinnitus.
These suggestions look simple, but when practiced regularly they can clearly change the person's relationship with tinnitus.
The NICE guideline also suggests considering screening with an insomnia scale for people whose tinnitus disturbs their sleep.
Sound therapy is the use of external sound to change the perception or the impact of tinnitus.
Its simplest form is sound enrichment: sounds such as a fan, nature sounds or soft music are added to the environment.
Sound generators, worn behind or in the ear, deliver a steady and adjustable noise.
Combination devices bring a hearing aid and a sound generator together in a single device.
The sound is usually set to blend with the tinnitus rather than cover it completely; this aims to support habituation.
The American guideline regards sound therapy as an option.
A Cochrane review, however, reports that the evidence on the effect of sound therapy is insufficient and inconclusive.
The NICE guideline also made no practice recommendation on this, only a research recommendation.
In sound therapy, the type of sound, its level and the hours of use are chosen for each person.
Broadband noise, nature sounds or music can be used; the choice depends largely on the person's preference.
The sound is kept at a level that is comfortable to listen to and not annoying.
In people who are very sensitive to sound, the level is chosen even more carefully and raised slowly.
The person uses the device or sound source at certain times of the day, especially in quiet settings.
Sound therapy is usually given together with counseling rather than on its own.
Most people with tinnitus also have hearing loss.
By amplifying environmental sounds, a hearing aid increases the input reaching the brain from the frequencies with loss.
This can make tinnitus less noticeable among everyday sounds, and communication also becomes easier.
The American guideline recommends a hearing aid evaluation for people with persistent, bothersome tinnitus and documented hearing loss.
The NICE guideline says to offer devices to those whose hearing loss affects communication, and not to those without hearing loss.
For mild high-frequency losses, open fit devices can deliver environmental sounds without blocking the ear canal.
Research evidence on the direct effect of hearing aids on tinnitus, however, is still limited.
Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, is the approach with the strongest evidence in tinnitus management.
This therapy targets not the sound of tinnitus but the thoughts, emotions and behaviors that respond to it.
For example, a thought like this sound will never stop and it will ruin my life increases anxiety.
Anxiety pulls attention toward the tinnitus, and the person starts to avoid social settings and activities.
In therapy, these thoughts are recognized, replaced with more realistic ones, and avoided activities are gradually resumed.
The American guideline recommends cognitive behavioral therapy for persistent, bothersome tinnitus.
According to a Cochrane review, this therapy can reduce the impact of tinnitus on life, but it has not been shown to reduce loudness.

adimlar.metin: One to one with a psychologist

cumleler: For adults who remain clearly affected despite support, the NICE guideline suggests considering a stepped psychological approach.
The first step is digital CBT, supported by psychologists and delivered by computer or phone.
If there is no benefit, group programs follow: CBT, mindfulness-based therapy or acceptance and commitment therapy.
The final step is individual CBT delivered by a psychologist.
The effectiveness of CBT-based approaches delivered by audiologists is still being studied.
So the audiologist should recognize people who need psychological support and refer them to the right place within the team.
Tinnitus management is often a team effort.
The audiologist takes on assessment, counseling, sound therapy and device fitting.
The ear, nose and throat physician carries out the medical evaluation and decides on any necessary investigations.
If there is marked distress, anxiety or depression, a psychologist and a psychiatrist join the process.
When team members speak the same language, the person does not receive conflicting messages.
Guidelines advise against the routine use of some common treatments for tinnitus.
The American guideline does not recommend routine antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics or intratympanic medications for tinnitus.
Ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc and similar dietary supplements are not recommended either.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation is also not recommended for routine use.
The NICE guideline also advises against betahistine for treating tinnitus.
Treatment of accompanying conditions, such as anxiety or depression, depends on the physician's assessment and decision.
Let us bring all these approaches together in a management plan.
The first step is an audiological assessment and a questionnaire that shows the impact of tinnitus.
The second step, for everyone, is education-based counseling.
If there is hearing loss, a hearing aid is added, and sound therapy if needed.
If the impact persists, a referral is made to the right specialist for psychological treatment.
Follow-up uses the same questionnaire at set intervals, and the plan is updated based on the person's response.
Every plan is different; for some people, counseling alone is enough.
There is active research on new methods for tinnitus.
Neuromodulation devices, which pair sound with stimulation of areas such as the tongue or neck, are one example.
The NICE guideline found the evidence for neuromodulation insufficient and made only a research recommendation.
Patients often meet online products that promise a cure, so we should help them judge these claims against the evidence.
When judging a new method, look for effectiveness shown in controlled studies.

sahneler.metin: Do not say nothing can be done and you must get used to it. Explain that tinnitus is common, most people habituate over time and methods exist that help.
cumleler: A clinical tip: in counseling, avoid sentences like nothing can be done, you just have to get used to it.
Such a sentence increases the person's sense of helplessness and does not match the approach the guidelines recommend.
Instead, explain that tinnitus is common, that most people habituate over time and that there are methods that make this easier.
Realistic and hopeful language increases the person's engagement with the management plan.

maddeler.metin: Hearing aids if there is loss

cumleler: The goal of tinnitus management is not to erase the sound but to reduce its impact and support habituation.
The foundation of all management is education-based counseling; the evidence for sound therapy is limited.
If there is hearing loss that affects communication, a hearing aid is an important part of management.
CBT has the strongest evidence; guidelines do not routinely recommend medications or dietary supplements.

sahneler.soru: Which approach has the strongest evidence?
sahneler.aciklama: It can reduce tinnitus's _impact on life_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which psychological approach has the strongest evidence in tinnitus management?

cumleler: The correct answer is A: cognitive behavioral therapy.
This therapy targets the person's reaction to tinnitus rather than the sound, and it can reduce its impact on life.
